title: binary search tree ordering, lookup, and mutation
concepts: A binary search tree maintains an ordering invariant across entire subtrees: values in the left subtree are smaller and values in the right subtree are larger, subject to a documented duplicate policy.
Search follows one root-to-leaf path by comparing the target with each node, giving O(height) time rather than guaranteed O(log n).
Inorder traversal of a BST yields values in sorted order; reverse inorder yields descending order and can stop early for order statistics.
Insertion follows search links until an empty child position is found and attaches the new node without changing existing node order.
Deletion has three structural cases: remove a leaf, replace a one-child node with its child, or replace a two-child node using an inorder successor or predecessor.
A plain BST can become skewed after ordered insertions, degrading search, insertion, and deletion to O(n); self-balancing trees address height through rotations and additional invariants.
Range queries can prune an entire subtree when its key bounds cannot contain answers; subtree-size metadata can support faster repeated rank queries but must be maintained on mutations.
Validation must propagate lower and upper bounds from ancestors; comparing only each node with its immediate children misses invalid descendants.
